challengeIndia approves dengue vaccine: Doctor explains the four virus strains and why immunity remains a major challengeAadya Jha / TIMESOFINDIA.COM / Updated: Jul 20, 2026, 17:41 ISTShareAA+Text SizeSmallMediumLargeFollow us 1/8Why dengue immunity is more complicated than you thinkMonsoon often brings relief from the heat, but it also marks the return of one of India's biggest seasonal health concerns: dengue. Every year, thousands of people assume that once they have recovered from dengue, they have little to worry about in the future. It sounds logical, but unfortunately, that is not how dengue works.Unlike many viral infections that leave behind broad protection, dengue is far more complicated. The virus exists in four different forms, known as serotypes or strains. An infection caused by one strain usually protects a person only from that specific strain, leaving the door open for infection by the other three.Read More2/8India's first dengue vaccine: What you should knowIndia has approved its first dengue vaccine, QDENGA (TAK-003), developed by Takeda Biopharmaceuticals India, for people aged 4 to 60 years. Given in two doses, three months apart, the vaccine is designed to protect against all four dengue virus serotypes (DENV-1 to DENV-4) and does not require pre-vaccination screening. While it offers broad protection and reduces the risk of severe dengue and hospitalisation, no vaccine provides 100% immunity against every infection or strain. Experts say vaccination should be taken according to national guidelines and should complement, not replace, measures to prevent mosquito bites.Read More3/8Dengue is not one virus, it comes in four different serotypesThe dengue virus belongs to a family called flaviviruses and exists as four distinct serotypes: DENV-1, DENV-2, DENV-3, and DENV-4. Although they are closely related, they are different enough for the immune system to recognise them separately.Dr Raj Kumar, Sr. Consultant, Pulmonary Medicine, ISIC Multispeciality Hospital, explained, "Dengue continues to be one of the most prevalent mosquito-borne viral diseases, particularly in the monsoon months. What many are not aware of is that there are four virus strains (serotypes) of Dengue. Once infected with one strain, long-term immunity is typically only established against that one strain. They may still become infected with the remaining three strains in the future, though."This is why someone who had dengue five years ago is not automatically protected today. If another serotype is circulating in the community, a fresh infection remains possible.Read More4/8Why a second dengue infection can sometimes be more dangerousOne of the reasons doctors take repeat dengue infections seriously is a process called antibody-dependent enhancement (ADE). Scientists believe that antibodies formed during the first infection may not completely neutralise a different serotype during a later infection. Instead, they may unintentionally help the virus enter immune cells more efficiently, increasing the risk of severe disease in some people.Dr Kumar said, "As a matter of fact, dengue fever can be more serious upon a second infection with a different strain of the virus. That's why it's still the best way to avoid mosquito bites, even after experiencing dengue."This does not mean every second infection becomes severe. Many people recover completely. However, doctors recommend taking every episode of dengue seriously, regardless of whether someone has had the illness before.Read More5/8If there are four strains, can one vaccine really protect against all of them?This is where dengue vaccination becomes more complex than vaccines for many other viral diseases.An ideal dengue vaccine needs to generate strong and balanced protection against all four serotypes. That is why dengue vaccines have undergone extensive evaluation, and different countries recommend different vaccines for different groups of people.Dr Kumar explained, "There is also a lot of debate as to whether one dengue vaccine will be sufficient to protect against all strains. The solution is not as simple as it sounds. Complete protection is required from all four strains of the dengue virus in an ideal vaccine, as incomplete protection may not be adequate."He further added, "Currently, guidelines for the use of dengue vaccines differ from country to country and are based on age, prior dengue infection, disease burden, and which vaccine is approved. Thus, vaccination should only be done after consulting a competent health expert and following the national health guidelines."Read More6/8Even after vaccination, mosquito protection remains essentialDr Kumar said, "It is important to recognize that a vaccine is not 100% effective in eradicating the risk of dengue. Simple preventive measures are also as important."He advised, "Individuals should be protected from the bite of mosquitoes by using mosquito repellents, wearing long-sleeved clothes, using mosquito nets while sleeping, and ensuring that there is no stagnant water around the house where mosquitoes can breed."Sometimes, preventing dengue begins with something as simple as emptying a forgotten flower pot tray or covering a water storage container. These small habits can interrupt the breeding cycle of Aedes mosquitoes before they spread infection.Read More7/8Know the warning signs, and don't wait for symptoms to worsenDengue often starts with symptoms that resemble many other viral illnesses. But timely diagnosis can make a significant difference, especially when hydration and medical monitoring are started early.Dr Kumar said, "If they start to become ill with a high fever, a very bad headache, a headache behind the eyes, joint pain, nausea, vomiting or rashes, they should go to the doctor immediately. The earlier the diagnosis, the better to prevent complications when it comes to hydration and timely medical care."He added, "Dengue can be treated successfully if recognised in time, but if not, it can worsen to a serious illness."Read More8/8Medical experts consultedThis article includes expert inputs shared with TOI Health by:Dr Raj Kumar, Sr. Consultant, Pulmonary Medicine, ISIC Multispeciality Hospital.Inputs were used to explain why dengue infection does not provide protection against all virus strains, why repeat infections can still occur, and why vaccination should be taken only after consulting a qualified healthcare professional.Read MoreFollow Us On Social MediaPhotostoriesFrom having no work for three years after quitting Sasural Simar Ka to wife Dipika Kakar's financial support; When Shoaib Ibrahim spoke about his struggles, career and lifeIndia approves dengue vaccine: Doctor explains the four virus strains and why immunity remains a major challengeLoved 'The Odyssey'? surge in dengue fever casesNext video inShareNextKEEP WATCHINGRelated: Brazil face surge in dengue fever casesSri Lanka has deployed military drones in its war against mosquitoes to tackle the country's worst dengue outbreak in almost a decade, which has already claimed 56 lives.The island nation has reported more than 77,000 infections since January, prompting Anura Kumara Dissanayake’s government to appoint a monitoring unit under the military.The National Dengue Control Unit has identified 162 divisions as high-risk areas for transmission.While infections have been reported across the country, the national capital Colombo has thus far accounted for the highest number.Health officials have blamed a more virulent strain of the dengue virus for the latest outbreak. The health ministry has now sought assistance from the armed forces to avoid a repeat of the country's worst dengue outbreak in 2017, when more than 186,000 people were infected and at least 450 succumbed.RECOMMENDEDMiquita Oliver opens up on her ‘awful’ treatment of fellow TV starWreckage of doomed Pan Am flight found on ocean floor 74 years after crash3 Common Cat Behaviors Most Owners Don't Realize Are Warning SignsDr. Marty | SponsoredSponsoredCostco Shoppers Say This Wrinkle "Serum" Is The Real DealHealthy Skin | SponsoredSponsoredopen image in galleryA dengue patient gets treatment at a hospital in Negombo, Sri Lanka (Reuters)The ministry has deployed air force drones to find stagnant rooftop pools formed by monsoon ⁠rains and pressed police officers to inspect homes, building sites and schools in a campaign to stamp out breeding sites of mosquitos. Hospitals added beds, set up special wards and extended duty hours for doctors and nurses to tackle an influx of more than ​18,000 cases ⁠in the first two weeks of July, health authorities said.Public health authorities attributed the increase in dengue infections to Cyclone Ditwah, which tore through the island nation in December, damaging critical infrastructure and health facilities. “A lot of debris was in our environment, so we noticed a lot of mosquito breeding places, and our entomological indices were high from that time," said Prashila Samaraweera, consultant community physician at the National Dengue Control Unit.The outbreak has strained resources in a nation of 22 million that has struggled to recover from years of economic decline. The recovery from the economic crisis, which sparked mass street protests that toppled the previous government in 2022, has not been helped by the energy shortage caused by the US-Israeli war on Iran.Public health workers were "stretched to their limit", Kapila Kannangara, acting director general of the dengue unit, said. "The number of patients is high, and the severity of the cases ⁠is high.”Nearly 75 per cent of the cases were linked to the more virulent DENV-2 strain of the virus, the official said, adding that it had a tendency to spread rapidly.open image in galleryA municipal worker fumigates a market area during a dengue prevention campaign in Colombo on 15 July 2026 (AFP/Getty)Health officials expect infections to ease off as monsoon rains weaken in August, but warn that they may climb back from November as rainfall returns to the island nation.Last week, authorities launched a drive to clean up the worst-affected regions, combing homes, shops and religious establishments to eliminate mosquito-breeding grounds. In all, the health ministry said, around 11,000 breeding sites had been cleared this month and fines issued to more than 4,000 premises found to harbour them."It's challenging for doctors because it's a rapid increase in patients," Lalindra Dias, a consultant in Negombo, one of the worst-hit areas about ⁠35km north of Colombo, said. "All of a sudden, ​you ⁠get a large influx coming into the hospital.” Mr Dias said his district hospital had treated nearly 1,800 cases in less than two months since June compared to about 1,050 in the same period last year.Sri Lanka recorded 8,590 dengue cases in May, 21,537 in June, and 21,650 cases in the first 20 days of July, according to the news outlet Ada Derana.To reduce pressure on hospitals, doctors are advising those with mild symptoms to recover at home."The doctor asked me to stay at home because ⁠my platelet count had not fallen too much," Shalini Aloka Perera, 23, told Reuters. “Then I did my treatment at home because ⁠there are too many patients in the hospitals."Dengue is spread by infected Aedes mosquitoes and can be serious in some cases. Mosquitoes typically lay eggs in containers that hold water, such as buckets, bowls, animal dishes, flowerpots and vases.Not everyone gets symptoms but if a person does, they usually start four to 10 days after getting bitten by an infected mosquito.RECOMMENDEDEasyJet chaos after mass brawl on flight from Tenerife to LiverpoolBlueface held at gunpoint after false claim he killed his girlfriendAlways Pour Olive Oil On Watermelon (Yes, It Works)Life Hacks | SponsoredSponsoredStudy Shows Surprising Link Between Aging & your PillowcaseBlissy | SponsoredSponsoredSome of the symptoms are similar to flu and can include high temperature, severe headache, pain behind the eyes, and muscle and joint pain. popoverPowered By 10 Sec 85 00Brazil face surge in dengue fever casesNext video inShareNextKEEP WATCHINGRelated: Brazil face surge in dengue fever casesSri Lanka has deployed military drones in its war against mosquitoes to tackle the country's worst dengue outbreak in almost a decade, which has already claimed 56 lives.The island nation has reported more than 77,000 infections since January, prompting Anura Kumara Dissanayake’s government to appoint a monitoring unit under the military.The National Dengue Control Unit has identified 162 divisions as high-risk areas for transmission.While infections have been reported across the country, the national capital Colombo has thus far accounted for the highest number.Health officials have blamed a more virulent strain of the dengue virus for the latest outbreak. The health ministry has now sought assistance from the armed forces to avoid a repeat of the country's worst dengue outbreak in 2017, when more than 186,000 people were infected and at least 450 succumbed.RECOMMENDEDMiquita Oliver opens up on her ‘awful’ treatment of fellow TV starWreckage of doomed Pan Am flight found on ocean floor 74 years after crash3 Common Cat Behaviors Most Owners Don't Realize Are Warning SignsDr. Marty | SponsoredSponsoredCostco Shoppers Say This Wrinkle "Serum" Is The Real DealHealthy Skin | SponsoredSponsoredopen image in galleryA dengue patient gets treatment at a hospital in Negombo, Sri Lanka (Reuters)The ministry has deployed air force drones to find stagnant rooftop pools formed by monsoon ⁠rains and pressed police officers to inspect homes, building sites and schools in a campaign to stamp out breeding sites of mosquitos. Hospitals added beds, set up special wards and extended duty hours for doctors and nurses to tackle an influx of more than ​18,000 cases ⁠in the first two weeks of July, health authorities said.Public health authorities attributed the increase in dengue infections to Cyclone Ditwah, which tore through the island nation in December, damaging critical infrastructure and health facilities. “A lot of debris was in our environment, so we noticed a lot of mosquito breeding places, and our entomological indices were high from that time," said Prashila Samaraweera, consultant community physician at the National Dengue Control Unit.The outbreak has strained resources in a nation of 22 million that has struggled to recover from years of economic decline. The recovery from the economic crisis, which sparked mass street protests that toppled the previous government in 2022, has not been helped by the energy shortage caused by the US-Israeli war on Iran.Public health workers were "stretched to their limit", Kapila Kannangara, acting director general of the dengue unit, said. "The number of patients is high, and the severity of the cases ⁠is high.”Nearly 75 per cent of the cases were linked to the more virulent DENV-2 strain of the virus, the official said, adding that it had a tendency to spread rapidly.open image in galleryA municipal worker fumigates a market area during a dengue prevention campaign in Colombo on 15 July 2026 (AFP/Getty)Health officials expect infections to ease off as monsoon rains weaken in August, but warn that they may climb back from November as rainfall returns to the island nation.Last week, authorities launched a drive to clean up the worst-affected regions, combing homes, shops and religious establishments to eliminate mosquito-breeding grounds. In all, the health ministry said, around 11,000 breeding sites had been cleared this month and fines issued to more than 4,000 premises found to harbour them."It's challenging for doctors because it's a rapid increase in patients," Lalindra Dias, a consultant in Negombo, one of the worst-hit areas about ⁠35km north of Colombo, said. "All of a sudden, ​you ⁠get a large influx coming into the hospital.” Mr Dias said his district hospital had treated nearly 1,800 cases in less than two months since June compared to about 1,050 in the same period last year.Sri Lanka recorded 8,590 dengue cases in May, 21,537 in June, and 21,650 cases in the first 20 days of July, according to the news outlet Ada Derana.To reduce pressure on hospitals, doctors are advising those with mild symptoms to recover at home."The doctor asked me to stay at home because ⁠my platelet count had not fallen too much," Shalini Aloka Perera, 23, told Reuters. “Then I did my treatment at home because ⁠there are too many patients in the hospitals."Dengue is spread by infected Aedes mosquitoes and can be serious in some cases. Mosquitoes typically lay eggs in containers that hold water, such as buckets, bowls, animal dishes, flowerpots and vases.Not everyone gets symptoms but if a person does, they usually start four to 10 days after getting bitten by an infected mosquito.RECOMMENDEDEasyJet chaos after mass brawl on flight from Tenerife to LiverpoolBlueface held at gunpoint after false claim he killed his girlfriendAlways Pour Olive Oil On Watermelon (Yes, It Works)Life Hacks | SponsoredSponsoredStudy Shows Surprising Link Between Aging & your PillowcaseBlissy | SponsoredSponsoredSome of the symptoms are similar to flu and can include high temperature, severe headache, pain behind the eyes, and muscle and joint pain. news.content_title: India approves Takeda’s Qdenga as first dengue vaccine
news.content: News Pharma & Biotech Academia Resources Login Sign up Sign Up India approves Takeda’s Qdenga as first dengue vaccine July 21, 2026•Approvals•2 Minute Read Takeda said India’s Drug Controller General of India has granted marketing authorization for Qdenga (TAK-003; dengue tetravalent vaccine, live, attenuated), making TAK-003 the country’s first authorized dengue vaccine. The clearance covers individuals aged 4 to 60 regardless of prior dengue exposure, without requiring pre-vaccination testing. The approval comes as India’s reported annual dengue case count has increased more than elevenfold over the past two decades, reaching more than 233,000 cases in 2024, although modeling indicates that the true disease burden is substantially higher. Qdenga is a live-attenuated tetravalent vaccine built on a dengue serotype 2 genetic backbone, into which envelope and pre-membrane genes from the other three serotypes have been substituted, generating four chimeric viruses intended to elicit immunity against all four circulating strains. Unlike Dengvaxia, Qdenga is authorized without requiring confirmation of previous dengue infection. The India approval draws on DEN-302, a local Phase III study, alongside the global pivotal Phase III Tetravalent Immunization against Dengue Efficacy Study (TIDES), described by Takeda as the largest and longest efficacy trial conducted for a dengue vaccine. Seven-year follow-up from TIDES showed sustained protection against virologically confirmed dengue and dengue-related hospitalization, although efficacy varied by serotype and participants’ baseline serostatus. In terms of the dengue space, Sanofi’s Dengvaxia, a chimeric yellow fever-backbone tetravalent vaccine, remains regulatorily approved in the US and EU for people with confirmed previous dengue infection, although Sanofi is discontinuing global distribution because of low demand. Brazil’s Instituto Butantan has also advanced a live-attenuated tetravalent candidate approved domestically for a similar serostatus-agnostic population. TAK-003’s broader label — usable without pre-vaccination screening — is the principal point of differentiation in this landscape, simplifying deployment logistics in high-transmission settings where serological testing is impractical at scale. Since its 2022 launch, TAK-003 has been authorized in 43 countries, including Indonesia, Thailand, Malaysia and Vietnam, with more than 32 million doses distributed through public and private programs in Asia, Latin America and Europe. The World Health Organization’s Strategic Advisory Group of Experts on Immunization has recommended the vaccine without pre-vaccination screening since 2023, and it holds WHO prequalification, enabling procurement through UNICEF and PAHO. Takeda said it will now work with Indian regulators and health authorities on rollout planning, though the company has not disclosed pricing, launch timing, or whether the vaccine will enter India’s public immunization program rather than remaining limited to private-market distribution. selected_identity.page_title: India approves Takeda’s Qdenga as first dengue vaccine

news.content_original: News Pharma & Biotech Academia Resources Login Sign up Sign Up India approves Takeda’s Qdenga as first dengue vaccine July 21, 2026•Approvals•2 Minute Read Takeda said India’s Drug Controller General of India has granted marketing authorization for Qdenga (TAK-003; dengue tetravalent vaccine, live, attenuated), making TAK-003 the country’s first authorized dengue vaccine. The clearance covers individuals aged 4 to 60 regardless of prior dengue exposure, without requiring pre-vaccination testing. The approval comes as India’s reported annual dengue case count has increased more than elevenfold over the past two decades, reaching more than 233,000 cases in 2024, although modeling indicates that the true disease burden is substantially higher. Qdenga is a live-attenuated tetravalent vaccine built on a dengue serotype 2 genetic backbone, into which envelope and pre-membrane genes from the other three serotypes have been substituted, generating four chimeric viruses intended to elicit immunity against all four circulating strains. Unlike Dengvaxia, Qdenga is authorized without requiring confirmation of previous dengue infection. The India approval draws on DEN-302, a local Phase III study, alongside the global pivotal Phase III Tetravalent Immunization against Dengue Efficacy Study (TIDES), described by Takeda as the largest and longest efficacy trial conducted for a dengue vaccine. Seven-year follow-up from TIDES showed sustained protection against virologically confirmed dengue and dengue-related hospitalization, although efficacy varied by serotype and participants’ baseline serostatus. In terms of the dengue space, Sanofi’s Dengvaxia, a chimeric yellow fever-backbone tetravalent vaccine, remains regulatorily approved in the US and EU for people with confirmed previous dengue infection, although Sanofi is discontinuing global distribution because of low demand. Brazil’s Instituto Butantan has also advanced a live-attenuated tetravalent candidate approved domestically for a similar serostatus-agnostic population. TAK-003’s broader label — usable without pre-vaccination screening — is the principal point of differentiation in this landscape, simplifying deployment logistics in high-transmission settings where serological testing is impractical at scale. Since its 2022 launch, TAK-003 has been authorized in 43 countries, including Indonesia, Thailand, Malaysia and Vietnam, with more than 32 million doses distributed through public and private programs in Asia, Latin America and Europe. The World Health Organization’s Strategic Advisory Group of Experts on Immunization has recommended the vaccine without pre-vaccination screening since 2023, and it holds WHO prequalification, enabling procurement through UNICEF and PAHO. Takeda said it will now work with Indian regulators and health authorities on rollout planning, though the company has not disclosed pricing, launch timing, or whether the vaccine will enter India’s public immunization program rather than remaining limited to private-market distribution. Reported cases have increased nearly 11-fold over the past two decades, and India accounts for almost one-third of the global dengue burden, although modelling studies suggest the actual number of infections is significantly higher than official estimates. Authorized for people aged 4 to 60 years, QDENGA is a live-attenuated tetravalent vaccine developed to protect against all four dengue virus serotypes. It is given in two doses, three months apart. Takeda said the vaccine can be administered irrespective of a person’s previous dengue infection and does not require pre-vaccination screening. Data submitted to the Indian regulator included findings from a Phase III clinical study conducted in India involving children, adolescents and adults between the ages of 4 and 60 years. According to the company, the vaccine was found to be safe, well tolerated and immunogenic in all three age groups. The approval was also supported by Takeda’s broader clinical development program, which comprised studies involving more than 28,000 participants from both dengue-endemic and non-endemic regions. Takeda said the vaccine recorded 80.2 per cent efficacy against virologically confirmed dengue one year after the second dose and 90.4 per cent efficacy against dengue-related hospitalization after 18 months. Follow-up data collected over the next several years showed continued protection, including 84.1 per cent efficacy against dengue-related hospitalization at 4.5 years and sustained protection against dengue disease and hospitalization through seven years across all four virus serotypes. The company said QDENGA has already been authorized in 43 countries across Asia, Latin America and Europe. More than 32 million doses have been distributed through public and private immunization programs. The vaccine has also received World Health Organization prequalification and is recommended by the WHO for use in dengue-endemic settings with high transmission. Takeda said it will now work with Indian regulatory authorities, healthcare providers and public health stakeholders to support the vaccine’s availability in the country.Vaccines & Immunizations Share With: No Comments Leave A Comment Cancel Reply Save my name, email, and website in this browser for the next time I comment. analysis_en.event: The Drug Controller General of India granted market authorization to Takeda Biopharmaceuticals India for QDENGA (TAK-003), the country's first dengue vaccine. The vaccine is a live-attenuated tetravalent vaccine designed to protect against all four dengue virus serotypes.
analysis_en.scale_impact_and_risk: Reported dengue cases in India have increased nearly 11-fold over the past two decades, with India accounting for almost one-third of the global dengue burden. Clinical data showed 80.2% efficacy against virologically confirmed dengue after one year and 90.4% efficacy against dengue-related hospitalization after 18 months. Protection against hospitalization was sustained at 84.1% at 4.5 years.
analysis_en.response_status_and_uncertainty: Takeda stated it will work with Indian regulatory authorities and healthcare providers to support the vaccine's availability. The vaccine does not require pre-vaccination screening and can be administered regardless of prior dengue infection. The approval was based on a Phase III study in India and a broader program involving over 28,000 participants.

Unlike some alternatives, QDENGA does not require pre-vaccination screening. Takeda plans to collaborate with authorities and stakeholders to ensure the vaccine's availability across the country.

The vaccine was confirmed to be approved on July 23, 2026, and the event is centered around Hyderabad, Telangana. The approval marks a significant step in dengue prevention, but no specific case counts, death counts, or exposure numbers are provided in the evidence. The response to this development is under investigation, with the focus on implementation and effectiveness. This decision is part of broader public health efforts to combat dengue, which is a major concern in the region due to its prevalence and impact on the population. The vaccine's introduction could potentially reduce the spread of dengue and mitigate its health risks, though further data and monitoring will be necessary to assess its full impact.

news.content: Sri Lanka Deploys Drones to Hunt Mosquito Breeding Sites Amid Severe Dengue Outbreak 21.07.2026 22:12 Text by : Editorial office news.by Colombo, July 21, 2026 — Sri Lankan authorities have deployed drones to locate mosquito breeding sites as the country grapples with its largest dengue fever outbreak in over a decade, which has already claimed 56 lives. Since the beginning of 2026, nearly 77,000 cases of dengue have been recorded across the island nation. In response, the authorities have established a special mosquito monitoring unit under the armed forces. The National Dengue Control Unit has identified 162 districts as high-risk zones for transmission. Colombo, the capital, has recorded the highest number of cases. According to experts, nearly 75% of infections are linked to the more dangerous DENV-2 strain of the virus, which spreads rapidly. The Ministry of Health has tasked the Air Force with using drones to detect stagnant water on rooftops, which forms after heavy monsoon rains. Police have also been instructed to inspect homes, construction sites, and schools as part of a nationwide campaign to eliminate mosquito breeding grounds. Hospitals have increased bed capacity, set up special dengue wards, and extended working hours for doctors and nurses to cope with the influx of patients. In the first two weeks of July alone, around 18,000 people were hospitalized. Scientists have linked the outbreak to the cyclone “Ditva,” which struck in December and caused significant damage to infrastructure and medical facilities. The resulting high humidity created ideal conditions for mosquito breeding. Разделы : In the world Ukraine Moves to Prohibit Russian Language in Public Performances and Arts 21.07.2026 18:57 Text by: Editorial office news.by Kyiv, July 21, 2026 — A group of more than 60 members of Ukraine’s Verkhovna Rada has submitted a bill that would prohibit the public performance and display of literary works, art, and music videos in the Russian language. According to the bill’s registration card on the parliament’s website, the proposed restrictions would apply even to phonograms, videograms, and music clips containing performances in Russian. The current Law “On Culture” already bans works by authors who are or were citizens of Russia, but it does not currently restrict the language of performance itself. The draft law also introduces stricter language requirements for public officials and private performers. Members of parliament, heads of state institutions, and individuals engaged in cultural activities would be required to demonstrate proficiency in Ukrainian. Candidates for elected positions, including the presidency, would need to provide an official certificate confirming their level of Ukrainian language proficiency. In addition, the bill proposes limiting the use of Russian as a language of instruction in private educational institutions. The initiative was submitted by a group of more than 60 MPs, including Nikita Poturaev, Chairman of the Verkhovna Rada Committee on Humanitarian and Information Policy, and Sergey Babak, Chairman of the Committee on Education and Science. The document has been referred to the relevant parliamentary committee for review. Over the past several years, Ukrainian authorities have pursued a consistent policy of reducing the presence of the Russian language in public life. Local authorities in various regions have already introduced bans on Russian-language books, films, theater performances, and songs. The study of Russian has been significantly restricted in schools and universities, and students are often required to speak only Ukrainian even during breaks. There have also been public calls to switch from the Cyrillic to the Latin alphabet and to distance the country from Russian cultural and linguistic standards. At the same time, Russian remains widely used by Ukrainian citizens in everyday life, and Russian-language music continues to be popular, frequently leading to public controversies. news.content: Bold News HomeLatest NewsTrending NewsEditor’s PicksIndiaJammu Kashmir NewsJammu NewsKashmir NewsLadakhEditorialOpinionMSMENationalEntertainmentBlogAbout UsContact Us Close the sidebar Sri Lanka Deploys Air Force Drones as Dengue Outbreak Crosses 76,000 Cases Authorities use drone technology and military support to identify mosquito breeding sites as hospitals struggle with a severe dengue surge. By Bold News Digital on July 21, 2026 Colombo: Sri Lanka has intensified its fight against a major dengue outbreak by deploying air force drones to identify mosquito breeding locations and support large-scale prevention efforts. The country is facing one of its worst dengue situations in nearly a decade, with more than 76,000 infections and dozens of deaths reported since the beginning of 2026. The outbreak has placed additional pressure on healthcare facilities, with hospitals witnessing a sharp rise in dengue patients. Health authorities have expanded preventive measures as the highly active DENV-2 strain continues to spread. Drone Technology Used to Locate Breeding Areas The Sri Lankan government has introduced drone surveillance to identify mosquito breeding grounds that are difficult to detect through traditional inspections. Air force teams are using aerial monitoring to locate areas where stagnant water may allow mosquito populations to grow. The initiative aims to improve early detection and support targeted cleaning operations. Authorities have also involved military personnel in inspection drives and mosquito-control campaigns across affected regions. Hospitals Face Growing Pressure The increasing number of dengue infections has created challenges for hospitals and healthcare workers. Medical facilities have expanded capacity to manage the growing number of patients, while health officials have advised people with mild symptoms to recover at home when possible. Healthcare workers are closely monitoring severe cases, especially those involving complications such as low platelet counts, dehydration, and internal bleeding risks. Climate Conditions Contribute to Dengue Spread Health experts have linked the rise in dengue cases to favourable mosquito breeding conditions following heavy rains and environmental disruptions. Authorities have increased public awareness campaigns, urging citizens to remove stagnant water from homes, workplaces, and public spaces. Officials are also conducting cleanup operations and imposing penalties in areas where mosquito breeding sites are discovered. Thousands of locations have already been cleared as part of the national response campaign. Public Cooperation Remains Key Health authorities have stressed that government action alone cannot control dengue transmission without public participation. Residents have been encouraged to maintain cleanliness, use mosquito protection measures, and immediately seek medical advice if symptoms such as high fever, body pain, or weakness appear. With continued monitoring and preventive efforts, Sri Lankan authorities hope to reduce the spread of dengue and ease pressure on the healthcare system in the coming weeks. analysis.brief_en: India has approved its first dengue vaccine, QDENGA, marking a potential milestone in the fight against the disease. Approved on July 21, 2026, the vaccine is expected to address the growing concern of dengue in the country. While specific details about the scale of dengue cases or the implementation timeline are not provided, the approval is hailed as a game-changer. This development underscores India's efforts to combat mosquito-borne diseases and could have significant implications for public health in the region.

news.content: People with type 2 diabetes face higher risk of dengue, warns review; experts weigh in A review paper highlights why high blood sugar may increase the risk of severe dengue and the warning signs people with diabetes should never ignore By: Lifestyle Desk 4 min read New Delhi Jul 21, 2026 06:00 AM IST Let's understand alla bout diabetes and dengue link (Photo: AI Generated) People with Type 2 diabetes face a higher risk of severe, life-threatening dengue complications, according to a review paper slated for publication in the International Journal of Diabetes & Technology , which calls for integrating dengue vaccination into routine diabetes care to protect vulnerable populations in dengue-endemic regions better. The study authors note that persistently high blood sugar impairs immune function and damages blood vessels, which makes people with diabetes more susceptible to severe dengue infection. According to the authors, such patients are more likely to develop an exaggerated inflammatory response, or a “cytokine storm”, which can result in dengue haemorrhagic fever, internal bleeding and, in severe cases, dengue shock syndrome, a potentially fatal condition marked by a sharp fall in blood pressure. DISCLAIMER: This article is based on information from the public domain and/or the experts we spoke to. Always consult your health practitioner before starting any routine. Diabetologist Dr Jothydev Kesavadev led the paper, which was co-authored by several leading diabetes experts from across the country, along with Dr Niti Pall, President-Elect of the International Diabetes Federation, Europe. “In India, there are more than 100 million people affected by diabetes. And among diabetics, there is a close to 2-4 times risk of developing heart attack, stroke, and multiple other infections and complications. Despite treatment, in 80-90 per cent of people, glucose remains high in our country. In our recommendation, we have mentioned that the dengue vaccine should be a part of routine care in diabetes,” Dr Jothydev told indianexpress.com . Here’s what you should note. Dr Rajiv Kovil, diabetes and obesity specialist at Zandra Healthcare, said that this is not a randomised trial but a review of existing evidence. “International observational studies and meta-analyses consistently suggest that people with diabetes who contract dengue have a higher likelihood of severe disease and possibly death. However, association does not prove causation, and the risk may also reflect age, obesity, kidney disease , hypertension or poor glycaemic control,” said Dr Kovil. Story continues below this ad Symptoms to watch out for. The initial symptoms are similar for anyone with dengue and include high fever, severe body aches, headache, pain behind the eyes, nausea, and skin rash. “However, people with diabetes should be particularly aware if they experience persistent vomiting, severe abdominal pain, unusual drowsiness, bleeding from the gums or nose, reduced urine output, dizziness, or sudden weakness. They should also check their blood glucose more often because infections can cause unpredictable spikes or, in some cases, low sugar episodes due to poor food intake,” said Dr Vijay Negalur, HoD diabetology, KIMS Hospitals, Thane. Hydration is crucial (Photo: Getty Images/Thinkstock) Prevention Prevention starts with avoiding mosquito bites by using repellents, wearing long-sleeved clothing, and getting rid of stagnant water around the home. Dr Negalur said that it is equally important to keep diabetes well-managed since stable blood sugar supports a stronger immune response . “Stay well-hydrated, eat balanced meals, and don’t ignore a fever that lasts more than a day or two. Anyone with diabetes who shows symptoms of dengue should seek medical advice early rather than wait for the illness to worsen,” said Dr Negalur. “Vaccination recommendations must follow approved indications and national policy,” added Dr Kovil. If someone with diabetes is diagnosed with dengue, are there any special treatment or monitoring considerations? Story continues below this ad Dr Negalur noted that some diabetes medications might need “temporary adjustments” based on the patient’s condition, appetite, and hydration status. “Timely medical supervision and regular monitoring of platelet counts, blood glucose, and overall health can greatly lower the risk of serious complications and support a smoother recovery,” said Dr Negalur. analysis.brief_en: A new review paper led by Dr. Jothydev Kesavadev highlights that individuals with Type 2 diabetes are at a significantly higher risk of developing severe, life-threatening complications from dengue infection. The study, slated for publication in the International Journal of Diabetes & Technology, explains that persistently high blood sugar impairs immune function and damages blood vessels, increasing susceptibility to dengue haemorrhagic fever and dengue shock syndrome. Consequently, the authors recommend integrating dengue vaccination into routine diabetes care for populations in endemic regions like India. While observational studies support the association between diabetes and severe dengue outcomes, experts emphasize that this does not prove causation. They urge patients to manage blood sugar levels rigorously, prevent mosquito bites, and seek immediate medical attention if symptoms such as persistent vomiting or bleeding occur.

news.content: Dengue fever and heart health: Expert warns of hidden cardiac risks to note The good news is that many of the patients with mild involvement of the heart recover well if the disease is diagnosed and treated early. By: Lifestyle Desk 4 min read New Delhi Jul 18, 2026 06:00 AM IST Dengue can also impact your heart. (Source: Magnific) With the monsoon comes mosquitoes, and mosquitoes bring with them the fear of dengue fever. Dengue is typically associated with high fever, generalised body aches, and a significant decrease in platelet count. But what many miss out on is the fact that the disease can also cause heart problems. With the increasing incidence of dengue in India, it has become even more crucial for doctors and people alike to understand that it is a multisystemic disease. Dr. Chirag D, a consultant in interventional cardiology, warns that while cardiac complications are not very common, they can range from minor issues to life-threatening conditions like myocarditis and acute heart failure. news.content: India has approved its first dengue vaccine, with the DCGI granting clearance to Takeda's QDENGA. Designed to protect against all 4 dengue virus strains, the vaccine is approved for people aged 4 to 60 years and does not require prior dengue infection testing. Ekta Batra explains. #Dengue #DengueVaccine #QDENGA #Takeda #Healthcare #PublicHealth #DCGI #India #Monsoon #HealthNews #WHO #CNBCTV18 #CNBCTV18Digital ...more Like Comment Transcript Transcript Transcript India has just approved its first dengue vaccine, and that's a big deal. Takeda's Queue Denga has become the first dengue vaccine to receive approval from India's drug regulator, the DCGI. Now, why exactly does this matter? Because India accounts for nearly one third of the world's dengue burden, and reported dengue cases have increased 10 to 11 times over the past two decades. Like we know every monsoon, hospitals prepare for a search in cases. So what makes this vaccine? Your friend Hugh Denga is designed to protect against all four dengue virus strains. It's a proof for people aged anywhere between 4 to 60 years and also it does not require blood test to check if you've had dengue before getting vaccinated. Takeda says the vaccine has been studied in more than 28,000 participants globally. In its phase three trial, it showed over 80% efficacy against confirmed dengue after 2 doses and over 90% efficacy against dengue related. Hospitalization at 18 months. The vaccine is already approved in around 43 countries and has been distributed more than 32,000,000 doses worldwide and is recommended by The Who for use in dengue endemic settings. The big question now is how much will it be prescribed in India, what will it cost and whether it will eventually be included in the public immunization programs. While this approval is a major milestone, Mosquito control. Eliminating stagnant water and preventing mosquito bites remains the first line of defense against dengue, according to experts

Despite this milestone, the cost and integration into public immunization programs are yet to be determined, while experts emphasize that mosquito control remains a critical defense measure.

analysis.brief_en: The Drug Controller General of India (DCGI) has cleared India’s first dengue vaccine, QDENGA, marking a significant milestone in the country's efforts to combat dengue. This approval comes as part of a broader initiative to address the growing threat of dengue, which is a major public health concern in India. The event, reported on 23 July 2026, highlights the regulatory progress in developing a vaccine for dengue, which is caused by the dengue virus. However, the news report does not provide specific case counts, death counts, or exposure numbers, focusing instead on the vaccine's approval. The DCGI's clearance suggests a positive response to the vaccine's development, but further details on its implementation, testing, or impact on public health are not included in the report.

India World Sport FIFA 2026 Data Health Opinion Science Entertainment Premium Videos Podcast Photos Visual Stories Specials TH Explains eBooks TH Games Newsletter Lit For Life The Huddle Home Sci-Tech Health QDENGA: India’s first approved dengue vaccine QDENGA, India’s first dengue vaccine, receives approval for use, marking a significant milestone in dengue prevention efforts.Updated - July 21, 2026 03:10 pm IST Zubeda Hamid0 / 0 NewREAD LATER SEE ALL Remove QDENGA, a vaccine for dengue manufactured by Takeda Biopharmaceuticals, a multinational pharmaceutical company headquartered in Japan, has received market authorisation from the Drug Controller General of India (DCGI). This makes it the first dengue vaccine to be approved for use in the country. The vaccine can be used in individuals aged 4 to 60, and is given in two doses, three months apart. It is designed to protect against all four dengue serotypes (variations of the virus). The company has still not announced an official price of the vaccine for India.About half of the world’s population is now at risk of dengue, with an estimated 100–400 million infections occurring each year, according to the World Health Organization. India, which accounts for about one-third of the global burden, is one of five nations that are are among the 30 most highly endemic countries in the world when it comes to dengue. news.title_original: QDENGA: India’s first approved dengue vaccine

analysis.time: Published July 21, 2026, at 03:08 pm IST; updated July 21, 2026, at 03:10 pm IST.
analysis.location_and_population: India; approved for individuals aged 4 to 60 years.
analysis.event: The Drug Controller General of India (DCGI) granted market authorisation to QDENGA, a dengue vaccine manufactured by Takeda Biopharmaceuticals, marking the first dengue vaccine approved for use in the country.
analysis.scale_impact_and_risk: India accounts for approximately one-third of the global dengue burden; the World Health Organization estimates 100–400 million infections occur globally each year.
analysis.response_status_and_uncertainty: The vaccine is administered in two doses three months apart and is designed to protect against all four dengue serotypes; the official price for the Indian market has not yet been announced.

analysis.brief_en: India has approved its first dengue vaccine, QDENGA, developed by Takeda Biopharmaceuticals. The Drug Controller General of India granted market authorisation for the two-dose regimen, which is approved for individuals aged 4 to 60. The vaccine is designed to protect against all four serotypes of the dengue virus. This approval is a significant public health development for India, which bears about one-third of the global dengue burden. While the vaccine's availability marks a step forward in prevention efforts, the manufacturer has not yet announced the official price for the Indian market.

While the vaccine's availability marks a step forward in prevention efforts, the manufacturer has not yet announced the official price for the Indian market.

Today, much greater emphasis is placed on preparing for health risks rather than merely reacting to them. However, efforts against vector-borne diseases like dengue and fever continues to be inconsistent with this idea prevention efforts tend to be spontaneous and responsive rather than continuing and preventative. Globally, mosquito-borne diseases kill more than one million people and infect up to 700 million each. Dengue has become hyper-endemic in the country. According to the report by National Center for Vector Borne Diseases Control (NCVBDC), as of September 17, 2023, 94,198 cases of dengue infection were reported in India. Mosquito breeding risks are rising each year, driven by climate change impacts and increasing urban density, which together are disrupting rainfall patterns and intensifying flooding. Despite increased awareness and coordinated mosquito control by public health agencies, prevention often focuses on peak transmission seasons. This raises an important question: can dengue prevention become less reactive and more preventive? Moving the conversation upstream Dengue management has traditionally focused on reducing adult mosquito populations once they become visible or disease incidence begins to rise. While these interventions continue to play an important role, increasing attention is being directed towards addressing the challenge earlier in the vector life cycle. This approach recognises a critical reality: stopping mosquito breeding early offers a more effective and sustainable defence against disease transmission. Today’s urban environment presents multiple conditions that support mosquito proliferation. Stagnant water in construction zones, rooftops, coolers, household containers, drains and neglected community spaces quickly become breeding habitats. These factors, combined with increasing population density and changing environmental conditions, highlight the need for earlier and more consistent intervention. From outbreak response to preventive action Building a stronger resilience against dengue requires multi-pronged approach. With changes occurring in the way that the disease spreads, there are increasing dependencies on environmental management, collective public awareness and innovation through science to assist in the prevention of dengue. Effective prevention is becoming more dependent on the collaboration of scientific innovation, environmental management, and public awareness as disease patterns continue to change. This logic has also influenced a shift to more integrated vector management solutions that are focused not only on addressing outbreaks but also on the mitigation of risk at its source. Beyond traditional prevention methods, there is a growing emphasis on new strategies to reduce mosquito populations earlier in their development cycle. Examples include naturally derived active ingredients from fermentation-based methods and a broader trend towards more targeted public health practices. However, creating lasting impact requires more than just innovation; it needs responsible water management practices and continued public participation to build healthier communities. Cleaner surroundings remain the first line of defence In addition to scientific innovation that is creating new ways to prevent disease, our daily actions are equally important. Routine activities, whether it’s cleaning up stagnant water, improving storage of drinking water, improving waste management, or routinely inspecting public places are part of the foundation of effective dengue control. The shared spaces we all use – our residential communities, schools, workplaces, governments and homes – all have a role in limiting the factors that allow mosquitoes to breed. Shifting from seasonal prevention to an ongoing public health effort, driven by awareness, accountability and daily habits, can help build a healthier environment. Building cities that prevent, not simply respond As India continues to grow and develop, there is a need to rethink how we design and maintain cleaner, healthier urban environments through a stronger public health lens, particularly in the context of dengue prevention. Achieving long-term risk reduction will require us to move beyond reactive outbreak control to a more proactive, sustainable approach. This includes creating cleaner environments and fostering community stewardship to ensure ongoing efforts to eliminate mosquito breeding grounds. Ultimately, success will not be determined only by how effectively we respond to dengue outbreaks, but by how consistently and comprehensively we remove the conditions that enable mosquitoes to thrive. We must create cities that prevent rather than respond. analysis.brief_en: A public health expert has called for a fundamental shift in India's approach to dengue control, moving from reactive outbreak management to sustained prevention. Published on July 22, 2026, the commentary highlights that dengue has become hyper-endemic in the country, with the National Center for Vector Borne Diseases Control reporting 94,198 cases by September 2023. The author argues that increasing urban density and climate change are exacerbating mosquito breeding risks, necessitating a move away from seasonal interventions. The proposed strategy emphasizes integrated vector management, environmental stewardship, and scientific innovation to disrupt the mosquito life cycle earlier. Furthermore, the piece stresses the critical role of community participation and responsible water management in maintaining cleaner urban environments. By fostering daily habits and shared responsibility, the author suggests India can build greater resilience against the disease and reduce the long-term burden on its public health system.

Every year, thousands of people assume that once they have recovered from dengue, they have little to worry about in the future. It sounds logical, but unfortunately, that is not how dengue works.Unlike many viral infections that leave behind broad protection, dengue is far more complicated. The virus exists in four different forms, known as serotypes or strains. An infection caused by one strain usually protects a person only from that specific strain, leaving the door open for infection by the other three.2/8India's first dengue vaccine: What you should knowIndia has approved its first dengue vaccine, QDENGA (TAK-003), developed by Takeda Biopharmaceuticals India, for people aged 4 to 60 years. Given in two doses, three months apart, the vaccine is designed to protect against all four dengue virus serotypes (DENV-1 to DENV-4) and does not require pre-vaccination screening. While it offers broad protection and reduces the risk of severe dengue and hospitalisation, no vaccine provides 100% immunity against every infection or strain. Experts say vaccination should be taken according to national guidelines and should complement, not replace, measures to prevent mosquito bites.3/8Dengue is not one virus, it comes in four different serotypesThe dengue virus belongs to a family called flaviviruses and exists as four distinct serotypes: DENV-1, DENV-2, DENV-3, and DENV-4. Although they are closely related, they are different enough for the immune system to recognise them separately.Dr Raj Kumar, Sr. Consultant, Pulmonary Medicine, ISIC Multispeciality Hospital, explained, "Dengue continues to be one of the most prevalent mosquito-borne viral diseases, particularly in the monsoon months. What many are not aware of is that there are four virus strains (serotypes) of Dengue. Once infected with one strain, long-term immunity is typically only established against that one strain. They may still become infected with the remaining three strains in the future, though."This is why someone who had dengue five years ago is not automatically protected today. If another serotype is circulating in the community, a fresh infection remains possible.4/8Why a second dengue infection can sometimes be more dangerousOne of the reasons doctors take repeat dengue infections seriously is a process called antibody-dependent enhancement (ADE). Scientists believe that antibodies formed during the first infection may not completely neutralise a different serotype during a later infection. Instead, they may unintentionally help the virus enter immune cells more efficiently, increasing the risk of severe disease in some people.Dr Kumar said, "As a matter of fact, dengue fever can be more serious upon a second infection with a different strain of the virus. That's why it's still the best way to avoid mosquito bites, even after experiencing dengue."This does not mean every second infection becomes severe. Many people recover completely. However, doctors recommend taking every episode of dengue seriously, regardless of whether someone has had the illness before.5/8If there are four strains, can one vaccine really protect against all of them?This is where dengue vaccination becomes more complex than vaccines for many other viral diseases.An ideal dengue vaccine needs to generate strong and balanced protection against all four serotypes. That is why dengue vaccines have undergone extensive evaluation, and different countries recommend different vaccines for different groups of people.Dr Kumar explained, "There is also a lot of debate as to whether one dengue vaccine will be sufficient to protect against all strains. The solution is not as simple as it sounds. Complete protection is required from all four strains of the dengue virus in an ideal vaccine, as incomplete protection may not be adequate."He further added, "Currently, guidelines for the use of dengue vaccines differ from country to country and are based on age, prior dengue infection, disease burden, and which vaccine is approved. Thus, vaccination should only be done after consulting a competent health expert and following the national health guidelines."6/8Even after vaccination, mosquito protection remains essentialDr Kumar said, "It is important to recognize that a vaccine is not 100% effective in eradicating the risk of dengue. Simple preventive measures are also as important."He advised, "Individuals should be protected from the bite of mosquitoes by using mosquito repellents, wearing long-sleeved clothes, using mosquito nets while sleeping, and ensuring that there is no stagnant water around the house where mosquitoes can breed."Sometimes, preventing dengue begins with something as simple as emptying a forgotten flower pot tray or covering a water storage container. These small habits can interrupt the breeding cycle of Aedes mosquitoes before they spread infection.7/8Know the warning signs, and don't wait for symptoms to worsenDengue often starts with symptoms that resemble many other viral illnesses. But timely diagnosis can make a significant difference, especially when hydration and medical monitoring are started early.Dr Kumar said, "If they start to become ill with a high fever, a very bad headache, a headache behind the eyes, joint pain, nausea, vomiting or rashes, they should go to the doctor immediately. The earlier the diagnosis, the better to prevent complications when it comes to hydration and timely medical care."He added, "Dengue can be treated successfully if recognised in time, but if not, it can worsen to a serious illness."8/8Medical experts consultedThis article includes expert inputs shared with TOI Health by:Dr Raj Kumar, Sr. Consultant, Pulmonary Medicine, ISIC Multispeciality Hospital.Inputs were used to explain why dengue infection does not provide protection against all virus strains, why repeat infections can still occur, and why vaccination should be taken only after consulting a qualified healthcare professional.Follow Us On Social MediaPhotostories10 traditional protein-rich dal dishes and calories per servingIndia has 5 Jantar Mantars, but only one is a UNESCO World Heritage Site; here's where they areWhy are chips packets filled with air? supplementary_news.content: Front Page Taiwan News Business Editorial & Opinion Sports World News Features Bilingual Pages SearchSearch All Front Page Taiwan News Business Editorial & Opinion Sports World News Features Bilingual Pages GO Home Taiwan News Tue, Jul 21, 2026 page4 New antibody offers possible dengue fever relief By Lee I-chia / Staff reporter Add TT as Preferred Source A research team from the National Health Research Institutes (NHRI) and National Cheng Kung University (NCKU) has identified the mechanism behind the severe inflammatory response triggered by dengue virus infection and developed a bispecific antibody that blocks it, showing promise as a treatment for dengue fever. The research team was led by NCKU Department of Medical Laboratory Science and Biotechnology professor Wang Jen-ren (王貞仁) and NHRI Immunology Research Center Distinguished Investigator Hsieh Shie-liang (謝世良). The team said an estimated 390 million dengue virus infections occur worldwide each year, with about 96 million people developing symptoms and approximately 500,000 progressing to severe disease, resulting in about 22,000 deaths annually. National Health Research Institutes president Sytwu Huey-kang, second from right, poses for a photograph with other experts during a news conference in the Ministry of Health and Welfare in Taipei yesterday. Photo: CNA In 2015, a DENV-2 dengue fever outbreak in Taiwan resulted in 43,000 confirmed cases and 228 deaths, the country’s largest dengue outbreak in decades. NHRI President Sytwu Huey-kang (司徒惠康) said at a news conference yesterday at the Ministry of Health and Welfare that dengue fever remains a public health challenge that is difficult to control. Patients might initially experience only a mild fever, but it is often followed by symptoms such as pain behind the eyes and joint pain, he said. In some cases, the condition can lead to dengue hemorrhagic fever or dengue shock syndrome. There is no vaccine to effectively prevent dengue fever, and clinical treatment relies mainly on supportive care, Hsieh said. During dengue infection, activation of immune cells drives excessive production of pro-inflammatory factors, contributing to fever, he said. The pathogenesis of severe dengue is widely believed to involve dengue virus-induced overactivation of immune cells, which triggers a cytokine storm. The excessive release of cytokines increases vascular permeability, leading to plasma leakage, dengue shock syndrome and organ dysfunction, he added. Hsieh said their study confirmed that the severe inflammatory response triggered by dengue virus infection is not driven by a single immune receptor, but by the combined action of two immune receptors.The team demonstrated that simultaneously blocking CLEC5A and TLR2 can effectively suppress the excessive inflammatory response caused by dengue virus. They designed and developed a bispecific antibody capable of targeting both receptors at the same time, he said. Wang said experiments showed that the bispecific antibody reduced various inflammatory responses associated with severe dengue caused by all four major dengue virus serotypes, as well as some strains carrying mutations linked to severe disease. The team said the antibody could be a novel treatment for severe dengue fever and might have applications against Zika virus and Japanese encephalitis. The NHRI said the research findings were published this month in the Journal of Biomedical Science. Separately, the Chiayi City Government Health Bureau yesterday confirmed the city’s first imported dengue fever case, involving a student who had returned from Vietnam. The student traveled to Vietnam during summer vacation and developed fever, headache and pain behind the eyes last Wednesday before testing positive for dengue fever on Saturday, the bureau said. The bureau sprayed the area within a 100m of the victim’s home, increased mosquito density surveys and removed possible breeding sites. It advised residents to eliminate standing water and take precautions against mosquito bites, especially during dengue season. Cambodian nationals will no longer be eligible for the Guanhong Project, which eases visa requirements for certain tour groups, or the Travel Authorization Certificate program, which offers conditional visa-free entry, MOFA said. In a news release, the ministry said Cambodia had failed to reciprocate Taiwan’s goodwill and had instead echoed China in statements undermining Taiwan’s sovereignty. The contamination was traced to two tainted downstream products, bringing the total number of affected soybean-based cooking oil batches to seven of the 30 batches produced by the company from April to June, the agency said. The tainted oil has affected a total of 1,322 businesses, it added.
